newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian debt seen reflecting low savings.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian debt seen reflecting low savings.

text.p: Australia's net foreign debt rose to more than A$200 billion at the end of 1996, but economists said the actual level of debt was not as important as the reminder of the need to improve the level of national savings.
Net foreign debt rose A$6.3 billion in the December quarter to A$202.367 billion from an upward revised September quarter level of A$196.042 billion, the Australia Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said.
"Today's data has no policy implications and as expected had no market impact," Westpac senior economist John Peters said.
It was the first time that net debt has been above A$200 billion, but economists said there was nothing of particular significance about that level.
"Despite the fact that net foreign debt has now cracked the A$200 billion mark, there are few significant implications from today's data," Commonwealth Bank economist Tim Moloney said.

The increase was made up an rise in debt financing of A$3.749 billion, as reported in Tuesday's quarterly balance of payments release, and other changes of A$2.920 billion. These increases were partly offset by a rise in the Australian dollar worth A$344 million.
The net debt financing increase mainly reflected foreign borrowing by the public sector, the ABS said.

The public sector's net debt rose by 8.6 percent to A$71.355 billion, while private sector debt rose 0.5 percent to A$131.012 billion. Public sector debt accounted for 35.3 percent of the net debt level.

The debt level also rose as a percentage of gross domestic product (GDP). At end-December it stood at 40.3 percent of GDP, up from 39.6 percent in September and the first time it has been above 40 percent since December 1993.

However, while rising as a percentage of GDP, debt servicing ratios improved, with the percentage of export earnings needed to service net foreign debt falling to 11.0 percent, a level well below its September 1990 peak of 26.5 percent.
While the quarterly rise in the debt did not cause much concern, economists said the level of debt was a poor reflection of Australia's savings performance, and improvement would not come quickly.
"Sustained improvement in the net international position will require a structural reduction in the current account deficit," ANZ Securities economist Phil Graham said.
The current account was a long term problem, and coupled with the rise in public sector debt, highlighted the need for the government to continue its fiscal reform.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economists said that "encouraging developments such as the present fiscal consolidation of the Federal government and the lift in the household savings ratio are much more significant than quarterly changes induced largely by valuation impacts."
